# Working with Files and Folders {#sec-file}

In @sec-read we learn to read data from files and write data to them. In this chapter, we will learn some other functions which are useful while working with files and folders. We can create, rename, copy and delete files, check whether a file exists, list the files in a folder, and create and remove folders, all from R. This is handy when an audit involves many files, like one file for each district or each month.

## Handling files

### Creating a file within R, using `file.create()`

Using `file.create()`\index{file.create() function}, we can create a new, empty file. If a file of that name already exists, it is emptied. The function returns `TRUE` if the file is created, and `FALSE` otherwise.

Example - The following command creates a blank text file in the current working directory.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.create("my_new_text_file.txt")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


### Checking whether a file exists, using `file.exists()`

Similarly, we can check whether a file of a given name exists, using `file.exists()`\index{file.exists() function}. Example-


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.exists("my_new_text_file.txt")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


### Renaming file with `file.rename()`

A file can be renamed using `file.rename()`\index{file.rename() function}. The basic syntax is `file.rename(from = "old_name", to = "new_name")`. It returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`, depending on whether the renaming succeeded. See this example.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.rename(from = "my_new_text_file.txt", to = "my_renamed_file.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Check whether old file exists
file.exists("my_new_text_file.txt")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


### Copying file with `file.copy()` function

Files can be copied from one folder to another using the syntax `file.copy(from = "old_path", to = "new_path")`\index{file.copy() function}.

### Deleting file with `file.remove()`

The function `file.remove()`\index{file.remove() function} deletes a file of a given name. Example-


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.remove("my_renamed_file.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


Let us check whether the file has really been deleted.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.exists("my_renamed_file.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


::: callout-warning
## Caution

Files deleted with `file.remove()` do not go to the Recycle Bin. They are gone. Never run delete commands on the folder holding the original data received from the auditee. Keep the originals in a separate, read-only folder, and work on copies.
:::

## Handling directories

### Get/Set path of current working directory using `getwd()`/ `setwd()`

The *working directory* is the folder in which R looks for files, and saves them, unless told otherwise. We can see its path with `getwd()`\index{getwd() function}.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
getwd()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "D:/OneDrive - A c GeM CAG of INDIA/new book - quarto"
```


:::
:::


Similarly, using `setwd("given/path/here")` we can change the working directory.\index{setwd() function}

> Note - The path must be given using forward slashes `/`. If backslashes `\` are used, as in Windows paths, each must be escaped with another backslash, like `"D:\\audit\\data"`, because `\` is itself an escape character in R.

As we will see at the end of this chapter, working in *projects* removes the need for `setwd()` altogether.

### Create new directory using `dir.create()` and other operations

A new directory (folder) can be created using `dir.create()`\index{dir.create() function}. For example, the command below creates a new directory named 'new_dir' in the current working directory. If `TRUE` is returned, the directory has been created.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dir.create("new_dir")
```
:::


We can check whether a directory exists using `dir.exists()`\index{dir.exists() function}, which returns either `TRUE` or `FALSE`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dir.exists("new_dir")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


`list.files()`\index{list.files() function} lists the files and folders in the current working directory, or in any other directory.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
any(list.files() == 'new_dir')
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


`list.files()` has some very useful arguments. `pattern` keeps only the names matching a regular expression, `full.names = TRUE` gives the full paths, and `recursive = TRUE` also looks inside sub-folders. For example, `list.files("data", pattern = "\\.xlsx$", full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE)` lists every Excel file anywhere in the folder `data`. We will use this to read many files at once in @sec-merge.

A directory can be removed using `unlink()`\index{unlink() function}, by setting its argument `recursive` to `TRUE`. Example


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
unlink("new_dir", recursive = TRUE)
dir.exists("new_dir")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


## Dialog boxes for selecting files and folders

We may use `file.choose()`\index{file.choose() function} to let the user select a file in a dialog box, and, on Windows, `choose.dir()`\index{choose.dir() function} to select a folder.

Try these in your console.

```
list.files(choose.dir())
file.copy(from = file.choose(), to = "new_name")
```

These are convenient for one-off work. For analysis that has to be repeated, write the paths in the code instead, so that anyone can see which file was used.

## Other useful functions for listing/removing variables

The function `ls()`\index{ls() function} lists all the variables in the current environment. The function `rm()`\index{rm() function} removes the given variables. The command `rm(list = ls())` removes *all* variables from the environment. Use it with caution, as it erases all data held in memory.

## Using `save()` to save objects/collection of objects

The function `save()`\index{save() function} saves R objects to a file on disk, for later use. The saved objects can be brought back with `load()`\index{load() function}. See this example.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
h <- hist(Nile)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
save(h, file="nile_hist")
rm(h)
any(ls() == 'h')
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
load("nile_hist")
any(ls() == 'h')
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


For a single object, `saveRDS()` and `readRDS()` are often more convenient. `readRDS()` returns the object, so we can give it any name we like, like `results <- readRDS("results.rds")`.

## Recording what data was received, file hashes {#sec-file-hash}

An audit conclusion is only as good as the data behind it. Months later, someone may ask whether the file we analysed is the same file the auditee gave us. A **hash** answers this. It is a short code calculated from the full content of a file. If even one character of the file changes, the hash changes completely. The function `tools::md5sum()` calculates one kind of hash, called MD5.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-01,1250", "PV-02,45600"), "received_data.csv")
tools::md5sum("received_data.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                 received_data.csv 
"1c8dff05a4b3c0d24ff45398a81d0308" 
```


:::
:::


Now suppose someone changes one amount in the file.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
writeLines(c("voucher,amount", "PV-01,1250", "PV-02,45601"), "received_data.csv")
tools::md5sum("received_data.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                 received_data.csv 
"36bdd89fc49c10e66e6ec7bd505a3d01" 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
file.remove("received_data.csv")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


A change of one rupee has produced a completely different hash.

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip

When data is received, record in the working papers the name, size and hash of every file, along with the date and the officer who gave it. Calculate the hashes of all files in a folder at once with `tools::md5sum(list.files("received", full.names = TRUE))`. The same idea is used for digital evidence in investigations. It proves that the data analysed is exactly the data received.
:::

## Working with Projects in `RStudio`

While working on a project, we usually want to keep all scripts, data, results, charts and figures in one place. RStudio has the concept of *projects*\index{Projects in R Studio} for this. A project is linked with a folder, and RStudio creates a file with the extension `.Rproj` in it. Opening this file reopens the project, with its scripts and settings.

To start a new project in RStudio, click the `File` menu, and then `New Project`. See the screenshots in @fig-proj1.

::: {#fig-proj1}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](images/Rproj1.png){fig-align='center' width=49% height=49%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](images/Rproj2.png){fig-align='center' width=49% height=49%}
:::
:::


Creating Projects in R Studio
:::

After creating the project, you will notice that a file with the extension `.Rproj` has been created by RStudio in the chosen folder.

To resume working on the project, either double click this file, or open the project from the menu, `File` $->$ `Open Project`.

In RStudio, we can create a project

- In a new directory (first option in @fig-proj1)
- In an existing directory (second option in @fig-proj1)
- By cloning a version control repository (like Git), as shown in the third option in @fig-proj1.

Working in projects, one for each audit or analysis, has many benefits over working with loose R scripts.

+ We never have to set or find the working directory. It is always the project folder.
+ All paths are relative to the project folder, like `"data/payments.csv"`. The whole folder can be copied to another computer, or shared with a colleague, and the code still works.
+ Results can be reproduced more easily.
+ Each project can have its own settings, and, with packages like `renv`, its own versions of packages.

A simple folder structure for an audit project could be `data/original` (the files received, never edited), `data/working` (cleaned data), `scripts`, and `outputs`.

## A suggested workflow

1.  **Start a project for each audit.** Create an RStudio project, so that the working directory is always the project folder and `setwd()` is not needed.
2.  **Set up the folders.** Use `dir.create()` to make `data/original`, `data/working`, `scripts` and `outputs`.
3.  **Store the received files untouched.** Copy the auditee's files into `data/original` and never edit or delete them there.
4.  **Record the hashes.** Calculate `tools::md5sum()` for every received file. Note the name, size, hash, date and the officer who gave it in the working papers.
5.  **List files in code.** Use `list.files()` with `pattern` and `full.names = TRUE` instead of dialog boxes, so that anyone can see which files were used.
6.  **Save results for later.** Keep intermediate objects with `saveRDS()` and read them back with `readRDS()`.
7.  **Check before deleting.** Use `file.exists()` before `file.remove()` or `unlink()`, and run such commands only on working copies.

::: callout-important
## Remember

Files deleted from R do not go to the Recycle Bin. Keep the original data in a separate folder and work only on copies. A recorded hash proves that the data analysed is exactly the data received.
:::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `file.create()`, `file.exists()`, `file.rename()`, `file.copy()`, `file.remove()` | base R | Create, check, rename, copy and delete files |
| `getwd()`, `setwd()` | base R | See or change the working directory |
| `dir.create()`, `dir.exists()`, `unlink()` | base R | Create, check and remove folders |
| `list.files()` | base R | List files, optionally by pattern and in sub-folders |
| `file.choose()`, `choose.dir()` | base R | Select a file or folder in a dialog box |
| `ls()`, `rm()` | base R | List and remove objects in memory |
| `save()`, `load()`, `saveRDS()`, `readRDS()` | base R | Save R objects to disk and read them back |
| `tools::md5sum()` | tools | Hash of a file's content, to prove it has not changed |
